# Chapter 14 – Air Made Useful

Arun sat in the environmental control station with three screens open and a tray of cold protein bars he had not touched.

The numbers on the left screen were the problem.

Tank pressure. Tank volume. Gas composition. Leak rate. Crew consumption. Sabatier output. Electrolysis yield. Reserve margin.

He had run the projection fourteen times in the last six hours. Each time the answer came back the same: comfortable now, uncomfortable later.

The base had seventy-two days of oxygen at current consumption. That assumed perfect recycling from the Sabatier reactor, which was not a safe assumption. It assumed no major leaks, which was a worse one. It assumed they kept the pressure at 55 kilopascals, which was the minimum for breathable air and already made everyone feel slightly winded during hard work.

Seventy-two days sounded like a lot until you thought about it in the right units. It was two and a half months. It was ten weeks until every tank in the base read zero. Ten weeks until every person in the linked modules started suffocating in their sleep.

Arun had been an environmental systems engineer for twelve years. He had passed hundreds of simulations, written protocols for a dozen failure modes, trained on the oxygen-loop mockup at Johnson Space Center until he could rebuild a CO₂ scrubber blindfolded. None of that training had prepared him for the moment when the spreadsheet showed him exactly how far the bottom was.

He pulled up the consumption graph. The colony was breathing roughly nine kilograms of oxygen per person per day. That was more than Earth because of the lower pressure. More oxygen per breath because the partial pressure had to be maintained. Twenty-one people meant roughly a hundred and ninety kilograms of O₂ consumed every day. The tanks held thirteen thousand kilograms.

Seventy-two days.

Then the numbers changed if the Sabatier dipped. Or if the electrolysis stack lost efficiency. Or if someone opened an airlock for too long during an EVA transition.

Seventy-two days could become sixty-six.

Could become fifty.

He pushed the tray of protein bars aside and stood up. The module smelled like recycled air. It always smelled like recycled air. That was the thing about closed-loop life support—you could never quite scrub the smell of yourself out of the air no matter how good the filters were.

Arun walked through the connecting tunnel toward the mess. The tunnel was twenty meters of ribbed fabric that flexed slightly when the pressure differential shifted. He had stopped noticing the flex during the first week. Now he barely noticed the sound of his own footsteps on the metal grating.

Jonah was in the mess, drinking water from a bulb and staring at a tablet.

"Oxygen," Arun said.

Jonah looked up. "What about it?"

"We have enough for now. Not enough for forever."

"How much is enough for now?"

"Seventy-two days. Call it fifty-two with safety factor."

Jonah set the bulb down. "That's tight."

"It's survivable if everything works perfectly. Nothing works perfectly."

"You're not telling me you want to cut the Sabatier temperature again."

"No. I want to stop thinking about reserves and start thinking about production."

Jonah leaned back. The chair creaked. Everything on Mars creaked after the first week. The temperature cycling and the pressure and the thin, dry air found every joint and seal and made them complain.

"Production from what?" Jonah said. "We brought one flight-grade oxygen unit. It's a breadboard. A toy."

"I know."

"How much does it make?"

"Three hundred grams per day. Maybe four hundred on a good power cycle."

Jonah did the math in his head. Arun watched him do it. That was the thing about Jonah—he did engineering math the same way other people tied their shoes. Automatic.

"Three hundred grams," Jonah said. "That's a toilet break for the colony."

"Less than one person's metabolic consumption."

"So we need something bigger."

"That's the conversation I'm starting."

Arun sat down across from him. The table was metal with a textured surface to keep things from sliding. Every surface in the habitat was textured or grippy or magnetized. Zero-G habits died hard even under gravity.

"Tell me about Mars air," Jonah said.

Arun smiled. It was a small, tired smile. He explained things for a living. It was the part of his job he was good at.

"Mars atmosphere is ninety-five percent carbon dioxide," he said. "About three percent nitrogen. One-point-six percent argon. Trace amounts of oxygen—roughly zero-point-one-three percent. Surface pressure averages six hundred pascals."

"Earth is a hundred and one kilopascals," Jonah said.

"Right. So even if Mars air had breathable oxygen—which it doesn't—you couldn't breathe it because the pressure is too low to drive gas exchange in your lungs."

"Good thing we're not planning to breathe it raw."

"We're not. But the CO₂ is useful."

Arun sketched on his palm with his finger. It was a habit. He drew molecular diagrams for people who did not speak chemistry.

"Carbon dioxide is one carbon atom bonded to two oxygen atoms. That oxygen is locked up tight. You need energy to break the bond. But if you have energy, you can split CO₂ into carbon monoxide and molecular oxygen. That's solid oxide electrolysis. It works at high temperature—about eight hundred degrees Celsius. You run current through a ceramic membrane. The CO₂ splits. Oxygen ions migrate through the membrane. You collect pure O₂ on the other side."

"How much power per gram?"

"It depends on the stack design. The flight unit draws about four hundred watts for three hundred grams per day. That's terrible efficiency. The stack is tiny. It's a proof of concept, not a production plant."

"But the principle scales."

"Everything scales if you have enough ceramic cells and enough heat and enough current."

Jonah was quiet for a moment. Then he stood up.

"Show me the unit."

The oxygen unit was bolted to a workbench in the environmental control module. It was about the size of a microwave oven. Stainless steel casing. Ceramic insulation. Power leads running to a dedicated converter. A gas inlet line from a small CO₂ tank. An outlet line feeding into the habitat's oxygen distribution bus.

Arun opened the casing. Inside, the stack was a cylinder of ceramic cells about the diameter of a soda can and half as tall. Thin. Fragile-looking. Each cell was a sandwich of electrolytes and electrodes and interconnects, designed by people who had never expected anyone to service it on a planet two hundred million kilometers from the nearest spare parts catalog.

"It runs," Arun said. "It makes oxygen. But look at the inlet pressure."

He pointed to a gauge on the CO₂ line. "It needs purified, pressurized CO₂ at ninety kilopascals. That means we have to capture Mars air, compress it ninety times above ambient, filter out the dust and the trace gases, and feed it into this tiny stack. The compressor we're using for that is a lab-grade diaphragm pump. It's rated for five thousand hours."

"How many hours on it?"

"Twenty-two hundred. And dropping."

Jonah ran his hand over the casing. His fingers found the weld seams, the bolt heads, the thermal breaks. He was reading the machine the way a mechanic reads a truck engine. Seeing the assembly logic. The compromises. The places where the design had been optimized for weight instead of durability.

"This thing was never meant to keep a colony alive," he said.

"It was meant to prove the technology works on Mars."

"It works. Now what?"

Arun closed the casing. "Now we build one that's a hundred times bigger. Maybe two hundred. Before the tanks run out."

Jonah turned and looked at the workshop module through the open hatch. The workshop was chaos organized by a person who understood chaos better than organization. Drill presses. Welding rigs. Hand tools in magnetic strips. A rack of salvaged compressor motors from the cargo that had been classified as "industrial spares."

"We have compressors," Jonah said slowly. "The big diaphragm pumps from the geological sampling rig. They were meant for moving Mars atmosphere through gas analyzers. Flow rate is decent. Pressure ratio is good. They're overbuilt for the original job."

"How many?"

"Three. Maybe four if I cannibalize the spare parts kit."

"Power draw?"

"Two kilowatts each at full load. Call it eight for all four."

Arun did the math. "That's manageable if we run them during peak solar. But the compressor is only part of the problem. We need the stack. The ceramic cells. The thermal management system."

"I can build the thermal system," Jonah said. "We have heating elements from the water purification rig. We have insulation panels from the cargo packing. I can repurpose a furnace controller from the materials lab."

"The ceramic cells are the hard part."

"They're the only part I can't make. But we have raw ceramic stock. We have the lab kiln. If I can cast and fire the electrolyte membranes—"

"You've never done that."

"I've cast rocket nozzle inserts. This is the same game with thinner geometry."

Arun looked at him. Jonah was not a man who made promises he could not keep. But he was a man who sometimes mistook difficulty for impossibility.

"How many cells do we need to hit production target?"

"The flight unit has six cells. It makes three hundred grams. To make thirty kilograms per day—which covers the colony plus a margin—we need six hundred cells."

Jonah did not blink.

"Six hundred cells. Each one about ten centimeters diameter. Stack diameter grows to about half a meter. Height maybe a meter. We're talking about a regenerative thermal enclosure rated for eight hundred degrees Celsius, with gas manifolds at each layer, current distribution across all six hundred cells, and a compressor system feeding filtered CO₂ at the right pressure and flow."

"Can you build it?"

"I can start."

They talked through the night.

Jonah sketched on a tablet while Arun pulled power budgets and flow calculations from the base engineering library. The sketch grew. A compressor bank pulling Mars atmosphere through a cyclone filter to drop the dust. Then a sintered metal filter for the fines. Then a cold trap to freeze out water vapor. Then the main compression stage—three diaphragm pumps in parallel, feeding into a surge tank. From the surge tank, the CO₂ flowed through a preheater, then into the ceramic stack enclosure.

The stack itself was the hard part.

Jonah drew it as a cylinder divided into six hundred cells. Each cell was a ceramic disk coated with electrodes. A voltage applied across the disk drove oxygen ions through the electrolyte. The oxygen collected on the outlet side. The residual carbon monoxide—the split-off carbon and the remaining oxygen atom—vented back to the atmosphere or got burned for heat.

"The thermal profile is the killer," Jonah said. "Eight hundred degrees at the stack. But the compressors need to stay below sixty. And the oxygen outlet has to cool down before it hits the distribution bus."

"Counterflow heat exchanger," Arun said.

"Right. But we don't have a counterflow heat exchanger rated for Mars atmospheric pressure."

"Then we build one."

Jonah laughed. It was not a happy laugh. It was the sound of a man realizing he was about to spend the next two weeks of his life welding something he had never built before, with materials meant for something else, on a planet that did not care if he succeeded.

"Power budget," Arun said. "Give me the full number."

Jonah tapped the tablet. "Compressors: eight kilowatts. Stack heating: four kilowatts steady-state, maybe twelve during warmup. Electrolysis current: another three kilowatts. Pumps, filters, controllers: two kilowatts. Total continuous: seventeen kilowatts."

"Seventeen kilowatts is half our daily solar margin."

"It's more than half during dust season."

"So we don't run it during dust season. We run it now, while the panels are clean, and we stockpile oxygen."

Arun looked at the numbers again. Seventeen kilowatts was real power. Real power meant real heat. Real heat meant real wear on every component in the loop. And if the stack failed—if a thermal cycle cracked a ceramic cell or a compressor diaphragm blew—they would have burned the power for nothing.

But the alternative was seventy-two days.

And then nothing.

"I need Elena to approve this," Arun said. "She needs to understand what we're risking."

Jonah put the tablet down. "What are we risking?"

"Time. Power. Confidence. If we build this thing and it doesn't work, we've spent seventeen kilowatts an hour for however long it takes to fail. That power could have gone to water processing. To the greenhouse. To charging the batteries for overnight survival. Every kilowatt-hour we burn on a failed experiment is a kilowatt-hour we can't get back."

"And if we don't build it?"

Arun did not answer. He did not need to.

They found Elena in the command module, reviewing Imani's latest ice survey data. The module was small—four square meters of terminal screens and a fold-down seat. Elena sat with her back straight and her eyes on the data, the way someone sits when they are trying not to show how tired they are.

"Oxygen," Arun said.

Elena looked up. "I saw your projection. Seventy-two days."

"Fifty-two with safety factor."

"I read the whole spreadsheet."

"Then you know we need a bigger plant."

Elena leaned back. The seat creaked. Everything on Mars creaked.

"The flight unit is a prototype," she said. "It was meant to validate the technology. Not to sustain us."

"I know."

"How much bigger do we need?"

"Two orders of magnitude," Arun said. "The flight unit makes three hundred grams per day. We need thirty kilograms per day minimum."

"That's a hundred times the output."

"Six hundred ceramic cells instead of six. Larger compressor bank. Custom thermal enclosure. No commercial off-the-shelf solution."

Elena looked at Jonah. "You've been thinking about this."

"I've been drawing it. Since about twenty-two hundred hours."

"Draw it for me now."

Jonah pulled up his tablet and walked her through the design. He did it without jargon, the way he always did. Compressors. Filters. Heat. Ceramic stack. Oxygen collection. Carbon monoxide vent. Power budget. Thermal management. He talked for fifteen minutes without stopping. When he finished, Elena sat in silence.

"Seventeen kilowatts continuous," she said finally.

"Yes."

"That's not a small ask."

"I know."

"If this fails, we lose a significant fraction of our power budget for the duration of the build plus the test run. We lose workshop hours that could go to other critical systems. We lose morale."

"If it works," Arun said, "we stop counting down. We start counting up."

Elena looked at him. Her eyes were red at the edges. She had been sleeping in shifts, like everyone else. But her voice was steady.

"What's your confidence level?"

Arun hesitated. That was the question he had been avoiding all night.

"I'm confident the chemistry works," he said. "Solid oxide electrolysis is proven technology. The Martian atmosphere is consistent. The compressor geometry is straightforward."

"But?"

"But nobody has ever built a six-hundred-cell stack in a machine shop on another planet. The thermal gradients during warmup could crack the ceramics. The gas manifolding could develop leaks that waste efficiency. The power conditioning could oscillate and damage the stack. There are failure modes I can't model because I don't have the data."

Elena turned to Jonah. "What's your gut say?"

Jonah did not look away. "We can build it. The question is whether we'll get the first thermal cycle right. If we do, it runs. If we don't, we crack cells and start over. We have enough ceramic stock for two stacks. Maybe three if we're careful with the offcuts."

"Two shots," Elena said.

"Two shots."

The silence in the module stretched. Arun could hear the ventilation fans cycling. The distant hum of the water recycling pump. The low-frequency thrum of the power converters. The base was alive around them, breathing and drinking and thinking, and every system depended on decisions made in this tiny room.

"Authorize the build," Elena said.

Jonah exhaled. He had not realized he was holding his breath.

"Full workshop priority," Elena continued. "You can reassign whatever labor and tools you need. But I want a written plan within twelve hours. Power budget. Timeline. Risk register. Failure contingency. If this thing breaks, I want to know exactly what we lose before we start."

"You'll have it by oh-seven-hundred."

"I want Arun on thermal modeling full-time. No other duties until the stack design is locked."

"I'll pull the data tonight," Arun said.

Elena nodded. She looked at the two of them for a long moment.

"We're running out of Earth," she said. "Every system we rely on came from the ships. Every replacement part, every consumable, every margin. This plant is the first thing we build that has to work because the imported version won't last. If we get it right, we breathe. If we get it wrong—"

She did not finish the sentence. She did not need to.

Jonah and Arun left the command module together. The corridor was dim, lit only by emergency strips. The base was on night cycle. Most of the crew was asleep.

"She's right about the risk," Arun said quietly.

"I know."

"If this fails, we don't just lose the power. We lose the confidence that we can solve our own problems. That's harder to replace than a ceramic stack."

Jonah stopped walking. He turned to face Arun in the dim light.

"Then we don't fail."

It was not a boast. It was not a promise. It was a statement of intent, stripped of all decoration, spoken by a man who had spent his entire life making things work in places where things did not want to work.

Arun looked at him.

"Seventy-two days," he said.

"Seventy-two days to build a factory that turns poison into air."

They stood in the corridor for a moment longer. The ventilation fans cycled. The base hummed. Outside, the Martian atmosphere drifted past the habitat walls at six hundred pascals, ninety-five percent carbon dioxide, waiting for someone to take it apart and make it useful.

Jonah turned and walked toward the workshop.

Arun watched him go.

Then he went back to the environmental station to run the thermal models one more time, because running them one more time was the only thing he could do until the sun came up and the welding started.

The sun would come up in four hours.

There was a lot of work to do.

*End of Chapter 14*

+# PART II — WATER, AIR, AND GROUND
+
+---
+
+# Chapter 11 – False Ice
+
+The convoy crawled into the airlock bay at 1417 hours local time, twelve hours earlier than scheduled. Nobody cheered. The hatches opened and the crew came out moving like people who had been holding bad news too long.
+
+Gabriel watched them from the inner door of the pressure tunnel. Imani was last out of the lead rover. She pulled her helmet off and stood there with her eyes closed, not saying anything, just breathing recycled air that smelled like other people's sweat and machine oil. That told him everything.
+
+The drill team had left at dawn the previous day with four rovers, two heavy drills, a melting rig, and seven people. They came back with three rovers—one had thrown a traction belt on bad ground and they'd abandoned it—one drill core in a sample tube that should have been full of ice, and a silence that spread through the base faster than any announcement.
+
+Jonah was the first to speak. He had come up from the workshop crusted with cutting fluid and metal dust, and he stood at the edge of the staging area with his arms crossed, reading the body language of the returning crew like a fault code.
+
+"That's it?" he said. "One tube?"
+
+Imani opened her eyes. "That's what came up."
+
+"Fourteen hours of drilling, two hundred kilometers of driving, and you brought back a sample you could fit in your pocket."
+
+"I know what we brought back, Jonah."
+
+"Then tell me what happened."
+
+The staging area went quiet. People stopped and turned. Gabriel felt the familiar tension—the kind that came when tired people needed someone to blame.
+
+Imani set her helmet on the rover hood with deliberate care. "The ground signatures looked right. Every spectral pass before departure showed consistent hydrogen returns. TIR anomaly matched what we'd expect from a shallow ice lens. We drilled to fifteen meters and pulled nothing but dry regolith with trace hydration. Secondary target, twenty-two meters, same result. The tool returns looked like ice. They felt like ice. But the ground didn't deliver."
+
+"The ground doesn't lie," Jonah said.
+
+"The ground tells the truth in a language we're still learning to read." Imani's voice was flat. Controlled. "We read the phonetics wrong."
+
+Mei stepped forward from the crowd gathered at the mess entrance. "What was the actual water content?"
+
+"On the primary core? 0.4 percent by mass. Bound hydration. Not extractable with our current energy budget without cooking the entire column."
+
+"Then we can't use it."
+
+"No shit," Jonah said. "That's the point. We burned seventy hours of collective EVA time, wrote off a rover we can't replace, consumed power we don't have to spare, and came back with a geological curiosity." He turned and pointed a finger at the ceiling, which was the direction of the surface. "We landed in the wrong place."
+
+"Aldrin chose this site," Elena said.
+
+She had entered from Command without anyone noticing. She stood in the shadow of the structural column near the rear pressure door, arms at her sides, voice calm in a way that made people pay attention precisely because it was so measured.
+
+"Aldrin chose it based on the best remote sensing data available from orbital reconnaissance," she continued. "Every survey, every lander mission, every radar pass for thirty years pointed to this region as the most water-rich landing zone in the northern lowlands. The decision wasn't a guess. It was the product of every space agency on Earth."
+
+"Then Earth was wrong," Jonah said.
+
+"Earth was working with satellite data from Mars orbit." Imani's voice carried an edge now. "Satellites see the top meter. Sometimes two, if the ground is dry enough. We're looking for ice at ten, fifteen, thirty meters. That's not a measurement error. That's a limitation of the whole approach."
+
+"So what's your excuse?"
+
+"I'm not making an excuse. I'm telling you what the science says. The hydrogen returns were real. The thermal signatures were real. But the interpretation was wrong. We thought it meant massive shallow ice. It meant trace hydration in a deep dry layer with a false thermal profile. The data didn't lie—we just read it wrong."
+
+Gabriel watched Elena's face. She was letting the argument run because she needed to see who would fracture first. That was how she worked. She didn't step into every fire. Sometimes she let the fire expose the weak points in the crew and only then brought the extinguisher.
+
+The weak points were showing.
+
+Hiroshi, the youngest of the drill crew, sat on a supply crate with his head down. He had been on Mars for three months and he looked like a man who had just realized the planet was bigger than his training. A woman from Life Support—Gabriel thought her name was Chen—stood near the greenhouse entrance with her arms wrapped around herself, the universal posture of someone who had done the math on how long the base could last without new water.
+
+Elena let it run another fifteen seconds. Then she stepped into the center of the staging area.
+
+"Enough."
+
+She didn't shout. The word carried anyway.
+
+"We are not having the 'wrong landing site' conversation. That's not a decision tree with useful branches. We're here. The ships are here. The equipment is here. The only question that matters is what we do from this position."
+
+"We need water," Jonah said.
+
+"I'm aware of what we need."
+
+"Then don't tell me we're not—"
+
+"I'm not telling you anything except what's productive." Elena's voice hardened. "Blame doesn't extract ice. Recrimination doesn't fill a single tank. I've seen exactly what happens to small teams under pressure when they start eating each other, and it doesn't end with more water. It ends with people making worse decisions because they're too busy being right at each other to be right about the problem."
+
+She turned to Imani. "What's your assessment?"
+
+"The site we chose has ice. Just not accessible ice. The bound water is real but uneconomical. We'd spend more energy extracting it than we'd recover, which makes the whole exercise thermodynamically stupid. But this region has more varied terrain than our initial surveys covered. We hit two targets. There are at least six more within range, plus three deeper anomaly clusters that the orbital data flagged but we didn't prioritize because the shallow stuff looked easier."
+
+"Priorities were wrong."
+
+"Yes. We chased the easy signature. We should chase the deep one."
+
+"Range?"
+
+"Hundred and forty kilometers northeast. The terrain is worse—rougher ground, more elevation change, probably slower travel speeds. But the signatures are stronger and deeper. If the deep model is right, there's a buried lens at thirty-five to forty meters that could be massive. Possibly hundreds of millions of cubic meters of accessible ice."
+
+"Possibly?"
+
+"Orbital data can't confirm thickness from that depth. It sees a density anomaly with the right dielectric properties. It could be pure ice. It could be dirty ice. It could be something else entirely that happens to look like ice in the sensor bands we used."
+
+"So another gamble."
+
+"Every drill hole is a gamble. The question is whether the odds are better than the last bet."
+
+Elena was quiet for a moment. The air handlers hummed. A pump cycled somewhere in the walls. Gabriel counted the seconds—nine of them—before she spoke again.
+
+"We expand the survey. Imani, you pick the three most promising deep targets from the existing data. We'll run a ground-penetrating radar transect to each one before we commit another full drilling operation. That costs time but saves the kind of failure we just had."
+
+"Ground radar adds four days per transect," Imani said. "Minimum."
+
+"I know."
+
+"And we still have the problem that GPR can tell us there's something there, but it can't guarantee purity or access until we put a drill string into it."
+
+"Then we'll have better data to decide which hole we take the risk on. Plan the first transect. Start tomorrow."
+
+Imani nodded. The tension in her shoulders didn't drop, but something in her eyes shifted from defensive to focused. She had a task now, and tasks were easier to carry than blame.
+
+The staging area began to break up. People drifted back to their stations. Jonah didn't move.
+
+"I need the robots," he said.
+
+Elena turned. "What robots?"
+
+"The prospecting units. Imani took four on the last run. Two didn't come back. That's three left. I need them for habitat expansion. We're still sleeping in three shifts because we don't have enough enclosed volume, and we're losing work hours we can't afford."
+
+"The robots are assigned to survey operations," Tomas said. He had appeared from the robot control alcove, tablet in hand, voice carrying the particular precision of someone who had already run the numbers. "That allocation was approved."
+
+"It was approved before the survey turned up nothing."
+
+"The failure of one survey doesn't invalidate the allocation."
+
+"It means we wasted resources we could have used building." Jonah's voice was rising. "I've got pressure shell sections in the cargo bay. Each section weighs three hundred kilos. I can move them with the sled, but I need robots to position and seal them. Without that, we're looking at manual handling—four people and six hours per section. We have eleven sections. That's two hundred and sixty-four man-hours I don't have."
+
+Tomas didn't look up. "The robots are running survey support. Survey support is water search. Water search is the priority."
+
+"Water search came back empty."
+
+"Water search came back with data. The next search has better targets. Canceling robot support now to save labor on habitat expansion creates a scenario where we have more volume but no water to fill a single tank. That's a faster death than sleeping in shifts."
+
+Jonah took a step toward Tomas. He was bigger than the robot engineer, and the movement was not lost on anyone.
+
+"You want to run that math again?"
+
+"I already ran it. I can show you the curves. At current consumption, with recycling at 92 percent and accounting for unavoidable losses, we have 147 days of usable water. Expanding volume adds 3 percent to daily consumption. Adding a second greenhouse adds 12 percent. Without new extraction within 90 days, we enter critical shortage. Habitable volume becomes irrelevant. You can't fill a larger house without water."
+
+"You're telling me my job doesn't matter."
+
+"I'm telling you building comes after survival. That's not personal. It's resource sequencing. If you want to argue with the math, argue with the math. But the math doesn't care about your feelings."
+
+"Tomas," Elena said. A warning.
+
+"I'm being accurate."
+
+"You're being accurate in a way that escalates."
+
+"Would you prefer I be inaccurate?"
+
+Elena held his gaze. Tomas held it back. He wasn't challenging her—Gabriel had learned to read the difference. Tomas simply did not recognize emotional arguments as valid inputs to optimization problems. It wasn't a character flaw. It was a limitation of his operating system, and on some days it was useful and on other days it made everyone want to throw him out an airlock.
+
+"Reassign two robots to Jonah," Elena said. "Temporarily. He gets them for forty-eight hours to get the first four pressure sections assembled. After that, they return to survey support."
+
+"Forty-eight hours isn't enough," Jonah said.
+
+"Then you'll have to prioritize. Get the sections that matter most done first."
+
+"Every section matters."
+
+"Then make them matter in order." Elena's voice had the finality of a sealed hatch. "Jonah, you get two robots for two days. Imani, you plan the ground radar transects with three robots instead of four. Work around it. I know both of you can, because if you couldn't, you wouldn't have been selected for this mission."
+
+She walked away before anyone could argue further. That was her signature—she didn't stay for the dying echoes of a decision. She made it and moved on, leaving the people who didn't like it to choke on their objections in private.
+
+Gabriel found Mei in the greenhouse ten minutes later. She was inspecting a tray of bean seedlings with the kind of attention that was really about avoiding other thoughts. The grow lights cast a pinkish-purple glow across her face that made her look tired in a way that went deeper than sleep debt.
+
+"Tough day," he said.
+
+She didn't look up. "Is there any other kind?"
+
+"Fair point."
+
+He pulled a stool from under the workbench and sat down. The greenhouse was the warmest part of the base, always a few degrees above the main corridor temperature, and the air was thick with the smell of damp soil and green growth. It was the closest thing to Earth they had left.
+
+"Can I ask you something?"
+
+"You're going to anyway."
+
+"The drill team did everything right, didn't they?"
+
+Mei's hands stopped moving. She straightened and looked at him with an expression that was half amusement, half something sharper.
+
+"Yes. That's the part nobody wants to say out loud."
+
+"Why not?"
+
+"Because it's scarier than incompetence. If they'd made a mistake—if Imani had read the data wrong, if the drill crew had missed a target that was obvious in retrospect—we could fix that. We could train better. Write better procedures. Buy better sensors. The problem would be in our control." She turned back to the seedlings. "But they didn't make a mistake. They did excellent science on excellent data and got a result that's useless for survival. That's the difference between research and colonialism. Research celebrates negative results. Negative results are data. They refine the model. They make the next experiment smarter."
+
+"And colonialism?"
+
+"Colonialism needs water. It doesn't care whether the data that misled us was beautifully collected. It doesn't care about publication. It doesn't care about the refinement of our geological understanding of the Martian northern lowlands. It cares about one thing: whether we can extract the resource we need before the reserve runs dry. Good science can still produce bad outcomes when the question is survival. Because survival doesn't grade on a curve. The planet doesn't reward you for having the right methods. It rewards you for being right."
+
+Gabriel sat with that for a moment. The grow lights hummed.
+
+"You sound like you've thought about this before."
+
+"I've thought about nothing else since I saw the crop yield projections on day three." Mei touched a seedling leaf. "I can grow the most efficient plants ever cultivated in a closed system. I can write papers that will be cited for decades. And if the water runs out, none of it matters. The plants die. We die. The papers rot in an archive nobody will ever read."
+
+"That's a cheerful thought."
+
+"I'm a biologist. I deal in truths that don't care about morale."
+
+She looked at him directly. Her eyes held something hard—a stubborn clarity that had made its peace with the odds without accepting the outcome.
+
+"The good news," she said, "is that we're not wrong about everything. The ice exists. The data was telling the truth about hydrogen. We just didn't understand the grammar. Next time we might."
+
+"Next time we have to."
+
+"Yes."
+
+Gabriel left her to her seedlings and walked back through the main corridor. Ship Two's interior had become the central spine of the colony—the place where people passed, where conversations happened, where the board on the wall tracked every critical resource in the settlement. He stopped to read it.
+
+**WATER**
+
+Import reserves: 12,740 liters
+
+Recycling rate: 92.3 percent
+
+Effective endurance: 147 days at current consumption
+
+Projected endurance with extraction failure: 134 days (accounts for degradation)
+
+Status: YELLOW
+
+Below the main board, in Imani's handwriting on the whiteboard underneath, someone had added a note in red marker:
+
+"Every liter we export for drilling is a liter we don't drink. Every liter we find is a liter we get to use twice."
+
+Gabriel stared at the numbers. One hundred forty-seven days. Five months. That was their runway. After that, the air would start getting thin in a different way.
+
+He walked to the Command module. Elena was alone, sitting at her console with a tablet. She didn't look up when Gabriel entered, but she shifted slightly, acknowledging him without words.
+
+"How bad is it really?" he asked.
+
+"Bad enough that I'm not going to pretend." She set the tablet down. "Jonah is right about more volume. Mei is right about more greenhouse. Tomas is right that the robots are the bottleneck for everything. Imani is right that the ice exists somewhere. Everyone is right, and everyone's rightness conflicts, and my job is to figure out whose rightness gets to kill us slowest if we bet on the wrong answer."
+
+"That's a hell of a job description."
+
+"It's the only one that matters on Mars." She rubbed her eyes. "The deep survey is the right move. But it's a bet. If the ice isn't there, we start talking about what a hundred-thirty-four-day survival plan looks like. And that conversation doesn't end well."
+
+"You think the ice is there."
+
+"I think the ice has to be there. That's not analysis. That's hope wearing a data coat."
+
+Gabriel sat down across from her. "I want to document the next survey. Not just the science. The crew. What happens when people are stretched this thin."
+
+Elena looked at him for a long moment. "You want to write the obituary before the death."
+
+"No. I want to write the evidence that we were alive while we were trying."
+
+That got something from her. A small shift at the corner of her mouth. Not quite a smile, but close.
+
+"Fine. But you stay out of the way. If Imani has to pull you out of a ditch, I'll lock you in the archive until the ice runs out."
+
+"Fair."
+
+---
+
+The next forty-eight hours were a controlled collision.
+
+Jonah took his two robots and worked sixteen-hour shifts assembling pressure sections. He slept in the workshop—Gabriel saw a sleeping bag unrolled on the floor next to the welding station—and he drove the robots with a single-mindedness that bordered on obsession. By the end of the second day, four new berthing modules were connected and pressurized. The base's usable volume increased by 22 percent. People slept better that night. Even the food tasted different, or maybe that was just the relief of having space.
+
+But the cost was visible. Two robots that could have been surveying ground were hauling wall panels. Three days of survey time lost while the colony got more comfortable. Comfort that wouldn't matter if the next drill came up dry.
+
+Imani ran her transects with the remaining three robots, working around the clock with a crew of four. The ground radar went out on the third day and came back with data that made her sit down in the middle of the staging area and stare at the display for a full minute without speaking.
+
+Gabriel found her there.
+
+"What is it?"
+
+She looked up at him with an expression he couldn't read. Then she turned the screen toward him.
+
+The radar profile showed a massive dielectric anomaly at thirty-eight meters depth. The signature was clean. Deep. Uniform. The kind of signal that textbooks used as examples of what a buried ice lens looked like on a ground-penetrating radar cross-section.
+
+"Is it real?" he asked.
+
+"I don't know." Imani's voice was steady, but there was something underneath it. A wire pulled tight. "It looks real. It looks exactly like what we wanted to see. That's what the last signature looked like too."
+
+"Then how do you know?"
+
+She stared at the screen. The lines of the radar profile were sharp and clear. They showed something underground that could save the colony or destroy it.
+
+"I don't," she said.
+
+She stood up and closed the display.
+
+"Tell Elena we're going back out. Tomorrow. Full convoy, full drill, full extraction rig. If this is ice, we bring it home. If it's false ice, we find out now, because we don't have time to run another survey."
+
+Gabriel nodded.
+
+"One more thing," she said.
+
+"What?"
+
+"Pack for a week. If this one's empty, I'm not coming back until we find something that isn't."
+
+She walked away before he could answer.
+
+Gabriel stood in the empty staging area, looking at the hatch that led to the surface. Outside, Mars was waiting. The same planet that had fooled them once, with the same tricks, the same sky, the same dust.
+
+They would go out again because the alternative was staying in and watching the numbers count down.
+
+They would go out knowing the data could be beautiful and wrong.
+
+They would go out with fewer illusions and exactly the same hope, because hope was the only fuel they had left that hadn't been rationed yet.
+
+*End of Chapter 11*

+# Chapter 14 – Air Made Useful
+
+Arun sat in the environmental control station with three screens open and a tray of cold protein bars he had not touched.
+
+The numbers on the left screen were the problem.
+
+Tank pressure. Tank volume. Gas composition. Leak rate. Crew consumption. Sabatier output. Electrolysis yield. Reserve margin.
+
+He had run the projection fourteen times in the last six hours. Each time the answer came back the same: comfortable now, uncomfortable later.
+
+The base had seventy-two days of oxygen at current consumption. That assumed perfect recycling from the Sabatier reactor, which was not a safe assumption. It assumed no major leaks, which was a worse one. It assumed they kept the pressure at 55 kilopascals, which was the minimum for breathable air and already made everyone feel slightly winded during hard work.
+
+Seventy-two days sounded like a lot until you thought about it in the right units. It was two and a half months. It was ten weeks until every tank in the base read zero. Ten weeks until every person in the linked modules started suffocating in their sleep.
+
+Arun had been an environmental systems engineer for twelve years. He had passed hundreds of simulations, written protocols for a dozen failure modes, trained on the oxygen-loop mockup at Johnson Space Center until he could rebuild a CO₂ scrubber blindfolded. None of that training had prepared him for the moment when the spreadsheet showed him exactly how far the bottom was.
+
+He pulled up the consumption graph. The colony was breathing roughly nine kilograms of oxygen per person per day. That was more than Earth because of the lower pressure. More oxygen per breath because the partial pressure had to be maintained. Twenty-one people meant roughly a hundred and ninety kilograms of O₂ consumed every day. The tanks held thirteen thousand kilograms.
+
+Seventy-two days.
+
+Then the numbers changed if the Sabatier dipped. Or if the electrolysis stack lost efficiency. Or if someone opened an airlock for too long during an EVA transition.
+
+Seventy-two days could become sixty-six.
+
+Could become fifty.
+
+He pushed the tray of protein bars aside and stood up. The module smelled like recycled air. It always smelled like recycled air. That was the thing about closed-loop life support—you could never quite scrub the smell of yourself out of the air no matter how good the filters were.
+
+Arun walked through the connecting tunnel toward the mess. The tunnel was twenty meters of ribbed fabric that flexed slightly when the pressure differential shifted. He had stopped noticing the flex during the first week. Now he barely noticed the sound of his own footsteps on the metal grating.
+
+Jonah was in the mess, drinking water from a bulb and staring at a tablet.
+
+"Oxygen," Arun said.
+
+Jonah looked up. "What about it?"
+
+"We have enough for now. Not enough for forever."
+
+"How much is enough for now?"
+
+"Seventy-two days. Call it fifty-two with safety factor."
+
+Jonah set the bulb down. "That's tight."
+
+"It's survivable if everything works perfectly. Nothing works perfectly."
+
+"You're not telling me you want to cut the Sabatier temperature again."
+
+"No. I want to stop thinking about reserves and start thinking about production."
+
+Jonah leaned back. The chair creaked. Everything on Mars creaked after the first week. The temperature cycling and the pressure and the thin, dry air found every joint and seal and made them complain.
+
+"Production from what?" Jonah said. "We brought one flight-grade oxygen unit. It's a breadboard. A toy."
+
+"I know."
+
+"How much does it make?"
+
+"Three hundred grams per day. Maybe four hundred on a good power cycle."
+
+Jonah did the math in his head. Arun watched him do it. That was the thing about Jonah—he did engineering math the same way other people tied their shoes. Automatic.
+
+"Three hundred grams," Jonah said. "That's a toilet break for the colony."
+
+"Less than one person's metabolic consumption."
+
+"So we need something bigger."
+
+"That's the conversation I'm starting."
+
+Arun sat down across from him. The table was metal with a textured surface to keep things from sliding. Every surface in the habitat was textured or grippy or magnetized. Zero-G habits died hard even under gravity.
+
+"Tell me about Mars air," Jonah said.
+
+Arun smiled. It was a small, tired smile. He explained things for a living. It was the part of his job he was good at.
+
+"Mars atmosphere is ninety-five percent carbon dioxide," he said. "About three percent nitrogen. One-point-six percent argon. Trace amounts of oxygen—roughly zero-point-one-three percent. Surface pressure averages six hundred pascals."
+
+"Earth is a hundred and one kilopascals," Jonah said.
+
+"Right. So even if Mars air had breathable oxygen—which it doesn't—you couldn't breathe it because the pressure is too low to drive gas exchange in your lungs."
+
+"Good thing we're not planning to breathe it raw."
+
+"We're not. But the CO₂ is useful."
+
+Arun sketched on his palm with his finger. It was a habit. He drew molecular diagrams for people who did not speak chemistry.
+
+"Carbon dioxide is one carbon atom bonded to two oxygen atoms. That oxygen is locked up tight. You need energy to break the bond. But if you have energy, you can split CO₂ into carbon monoxide and molecular oxygen. That's solid oxide electrolysis. It works at high temperature—about eight hundred degrees Celsius. You run current through a ceramic membrane. The CO₂ splits. Oxygen ions migrate through the membrane. You collect pure O₂ on the other side."
+
+"How much power per gram?"
+
+"It depends on the stack design. The flight unit draws about four hundred watts for three hundred grams per day. That's terrible efficiency. The stack is tiny. It's a proof of concept, not a production plant."
+
+"But the principle scales."
+
+"Everything scales if you have enough ceramic cells and enough heat and enough current."
+
+Jonah was quiet for a moment. Then he stood up.
+
+"Show me the unit."
+
+The oxygen unit was bolted to a workbench in the environmental control module. It was about the size of a microwave oven. Stainless steel casing. Ceramic insulation. Power leads running to a dedicated converter. A gas inlet line from a small CO₂ tank. An outlet line feeding into the habitat's oxygen distribution bus.
+
+Arun opened the casing. Inside, the stack was a cylinder of ceramic cells about the diameter of a soda can and half as tall. Thin. Fragile-looking. Each cell was a sandwich of electrolytes and electrodes and interconnects, designed by people who had never expected anyone to service it on a planet two hundred million kilometers from the nearest spare parts catalog.
+
+"It runs," Arun said. "It makes oxygen. But look at the inlet pressure."
+
+He pointed to a gauge on the CO₂ line. "It needs purified, pressurized CO₂ at ninety kilopascals. That means we have to capture Mars air, compress it ninety times above ambient, filter out the dust and the trace gases, and feed it into this tiny stack. The compressor we're using for that is a lab-grade diaphragm pump. It's rated for five thousand hours."
+
+"How many hours on it?"
+
+"Twenty-two hundred. And dropping."
+
+Jonah ran his hand over the casing. His fingers found the weld seams, the bolt heads, the thermal breaks. He was reading the machine the way a mechanic reads a truck engine. Seeing the assembly logic. The compromises. The places where the design had been optimized for weight instead of durability.
+
+"This thing was never meant to keep a colony alive," he said.
+
+"It was meant to prove the technology works on Mars."
+
+"It works. Now what?"
+
+Arun closed the casing. "Now we build one that's a hundred times bigger. Maybe two hundred. Before the tanks run out."
+
+Jonah turned and looked at the workshop module through the open hatch. The workshop was chaos organized by a person who understood chaos better than organization. Drill presses. Welding rigs. Hand tools in magnetic strips. A rack of salvaged compressor motors from the cargo that had been classified as "industrial spares."
+
+"We have compressors," Jonah said slowly. "The big diaphragm pumps from the geological sampling rig. They were meant for moving Mars atmosphere through gas analyzers. Flow rate is decent. Pressure ratio is good. They're overbuilt for the original job."
+
+"How many?"
+
+"Three. Maybe four if I cannibalize the spare parts kit."
+
+"Power draw?"
+
+"Two kilowatts each at full load. Call it eight for all four."
+
+Arun did the math. "That's manageable if we run them during peak solar. But the compressor is only part of the problem. We need the stack. The ceramic cells. The thermal management system."
+
+"I can build the thermal system," Jonah said. "We have heating elements from the water purification rig. We have insulation panels from the cargo packing. I can repurpose a furnace controller from the materials lab."
+
+"The ceramic cells are the hard part."
+
+"They're the only part I can't make. But we have raw ceramic stock. We have the lab kiln. If I can cast and fire the electrolyte membranes—"
+
+"You've never done that."
+
+"I've cast rocket nozzle inserts. This is the same game with thinner geometry."
+
+Arun looked at him. Jonah was not a man who made promises he could not keep. But he was a man who sometimes mistook difficulty for impossibility.
+
+"How many cells do we need to hit production target?"
+

   856|
   857|"I don't," she said.
   858|
   859|She stood up and closed the display.

   864|
   865|"One more thing," she said.
   866|
   867|"What?"

   869|"Pack for a week. If this one's empty, I'm not coming back until we find something that isn't."

   871|She walked away before he could answer.

# Manuscript Restoration Skill

## Purpose
Restore missing or incorrect chapter headers in a manuscript by comparing the Table of Contents (TOC) with the actual content structure. This skill is useful when importing manuscripts from various sources where formatting may be inconsistent or headers may be missing.

## When to Use
- When the TOC shows chapters that don't match the actual content structure
- When chapter headers are missing or incorrectly formatted
- When preparing a manuscript for publication or conversion to other formats

## Approach

### 1. **Analyze the Current State**
```python
# Read the manuscript file
content = read_file(path)

# Extract TOC entries using regex
toc_pattern = r'Chapter \d+: [^\n]+'
toc_entries = re.findall(toc_pattern, content)

# Extract actual chapter headers
chapter_pattern = r'^# Chapter \d+: [^\n]+'
actual_chapters = re.findall(chapter_pattern, content, re.MULTILINE)
```

### 2. **Identify Missing Chapters**
```python
# Compare TOC with actual chapters
toc_set = set(toc_entries)
actual_set = set(actual_chapters)
missing_chapters = toc_set - actual_set

if missing_chapters:
    print(f"❌ Missing {len(missing_chapters)} chapters")
    for chapter in missing_chapters:
        print(f"  - {chapter}")
else:
    print("✅ All chapters present")
```

### 3. **Restore Missing Headers**
```python
# For each missing chapter, find where it should be inserted
for chapter in missing_chapters:
    # Extract chapter number
    chapter_num = chapter.split(':')[0].split()[1]
    
    # Search for content that belongs to this chapter
    search_pattern = rf'Chapter {chapter_num}[\s:\-]'
    
    for i, line in enumerate(lines):
        if re.search(search_pattern, line) and not line.startswith('#'):
            # Insert header before this line
            header = f"# {chapter}"
            lines.insert(i, header)
            break
```

### 4. **Verify Restoration**
```python
# Re-extract chapters to verify
restored_chapters = re.findall(chapter_pattern, new_content, re.MULTILINE)
print(f"✅ Restored {len(restored_chapters)} chapters")
```

## Key Considerations
- **Backup First**: Always create a backup of the original file before making changes
- **Pattern Matching**: Use regex to identify chapter numbers and content boundaries
- **Order Matters**: Insert chapters in the order they appear in the TOC
- **Handle Duplicates**: Watch for duplicate chapter numbers (e.g., two Chapter 10s)

## Tools Required
- `read_file` - to read manuscript content
- `write_file` - to save restored manuscript
- `execute_code` - for Python processing
- `search_files` - optional for finding content patterns

## Success Criteria
- All TOC chapters are present in the content with proper headers
- Chapter headers follow a consistent format (e.g., `# Chapter X: Title`)
- No duplicate or orphaned content sections
- The manuscript flows logically from chapter to chapter

## Limitations
- Works best with manuscripts that have a clear TOC structure
- May not work well with highly irregular formatting
- Requires the content for each chapter to be present somewhere in the file

## Example Usage
```python
# Restore missing chapters in a manuscript
skill = load_skill('manuscript-restoration')
skill.restore_chapters(
    file_path='/path/to/manuscript.md',
    toc_pattern=r'Chapter \d+: [^\n]+'
)
```

## When to Use This Skill

Use this skill when:

## Workflow Steps

### 1. Survey the Manuscript Structure

Read the main manuscript to understand:
- **Heading hierarchy**: What level are part headings (`#` or `##`)? What level are chapter headings?
- **Part boundaries**: Where does the current content end? Which part should the new chapters go into?
- **Placeholder chapters**: Are there chapters that exist as outlines but not full prose? Where are they located?


### 2. Read the Source Chapter Files

Read each chapter file to be inserted:

```bash
# Read the files with read_file (preferred) or terminal
```

### 3. Choose the Insertion Strategy

Three common patterns:

**Pattern A: Append after last completed chapter** (most common)
The manuscript has Chapters 1-8 complete. Chapters 9-10 exist as outlines. Chapters 11 and 14 are ready. Insert after Chapter 8:

```python
# Insert after the "End of Chapter X" marker, before the placeholder section
insertion_point = manuscript.find("*End of Chapter 8 — Bridge:*")
if insertion_point >= 0:
    # Find the end of this line
    line_end = manuscript.find("\n", insertion_point)
    insertion_point = line_end  # Insert AFTER the end-of-chapter marker
```

**Pattern B: Insert between existing placeholder markers**
Placeholder comments already exist showing where outlines should go. Insert the chapter file content between or replacing the placeholders.

**Pattern C: Insert into a specific part with renumbering**
If chapters need renumbering, use `re.sub` with sequential renumbering. Note: this is uncommon for fiction; renumbering is covered by `publishing-workflow` §3E for non-fiction.

### 4. Preserve Part Headings

When chapters belong to a new part (e.g., Part II — WATER, AIR, AND GROUND that hasn't been written into the manuscript yet):

```markdown
---
# PART II — WATER, AIR, AND GROUND
---
```

- Match the existing part heading style (e.g., `# PART X — TITLE` with em-dash)
- Add the standard separator (`---`) before and after
- Use the same heading level as existing part headings (typically `#` H1 for parts)

### 5. Match Heading Conventions

**Critical**: Chapter headings in the manuscript MUST match the existing convention. Check the level used by existing chapters:

```python
# Check heading level — manuscript may use ## (H2) not # (H1)
header_pattern = re.compile(r'^#{1,3} Chapter', re.MULTILINE)
# Returns e.g. '##' if all chapters use H2
```

Common fiction conventions:
- Part headings: `# PART I — TITLE` (H1)
- Chapter headings: `## Chapter N — Title` (H2) — most common for fiction
- Title separator: `—` (em dash), `:` (colon), or `–` (en dash)

### 6. Add Placeholder Markers

For chapters that exist as outlines but haven't been written yet, add clear HTML comment markers:

```markdown

<!-- ============================================================ -->
<!--                                                              -->
<!-- Chapters 9 and 10 currently exist as outlines (not full      -->
<!-- prose). Insert them here when written.                       -->
<!--                                                              -->
<!-- ============================================================ -->
```

This makes it obvious where missing chapters go without breaking the markdown rendering.

1. **Read the chapter heading** — the file may start with `# Chapter N – Title` but the manuscript uses `##`. Adjust level.
2. **Insert the full prose** with appropriate heading level
3. **Add the end marker** — match the existing convention (`*End of Chapter X*` or `*End of Chapter X — Bridge: ...*`)
4. **Add separators** — use `---` between chapters

```python
new_section = f"""

{content}

*End of Chapter {num}*

```

```bash
      new_string="*End of Chapter 8 — Bridge: ...*\n\n---\n\n...new content..."
```

If the insertion point is unique, use `patch` with `replace` mode. For very large insertions, `write_file` may be simpler.

Check that the final manuscript is well-formed:

```bash

grep -n '^#' /path/to/manuscript.md

# Verify word count isn't drastically wrong
wc -l -w /path/to/manuscript.md

# Spot-check beginning, middle, and end of inserted chapters
```

Key verifications:
- [ ] Part heading level matches existing convention
- [ ] Chapter heading level matches existing convention
- [ ] Chapter separator style matches existing convention
- [ ] End-of-chapter markers match existing convention
- [ ] All original chapters are preserved (no deletions)
- [ ] Inserted chapters appear in the correct position
- [ ] Placeholder markers are present for outline-only chapters

## Pitfalls to Avoid

| Pitfall | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| **Heading level mismatch** | Existing chapters use `##` (H2) but insertion uses `#` (H1) — always check `grep -n '^#'` first |
| **Title separator mismatch** | Manuscript uses `—` (em dash) but chapter file uses `–` (en dash) — normalize to the manuscript's convention |
| **Deleting end-of-chapter markers** | When inserting after the last chapter, don't overwrite its end marker — insert AFTER it |
| **Missing part boundary** | If chapters belong to a new part, add the part heading before them with proper separators |
| **Overlapping with placeholder chapters** | If chapters 9-10 are placeholders, don't accidentally overwrite or skip them — insert after them |
| **Renumbering when unnecessary** | These chapters are already numbered (11, 14). Don't renumber unless explicitly asked |
| **Patching the wrong anchor** | Verify the patch anchor string is unique in the file before using it |
| **Forgetting placeholders for unwritten chapters** | Always add visible markers so the next writer knows where to insert |

